items.title: Learner Autonomy and Critical Thinking in AI-Assisted Adult Learning
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly entering adult and continuing education, where it can explain, summarise, draft and evaluate on the learner's behalf. The quality of work produced with AI assistance may therefore rise while the learner's own understanding, judgement and critical thinking remain unchanged or decline. This conceptual article examines how AI-assisted adult learning can preserve learner autonomy, independent judgement and critical thinking while still benefiting from generative tools. It builds on Natseva's distinction between functional cognitive offloading and higher-order cognitive outsourcing and integrates it with research on learner autonomy, self-regulated learning, metacognition, automation bias, critical-thinking instruction and the learning–performance distinction, drawing on a purposive, non-systematic literature selection that is reported transparently. Because most empirical studies of generative AI in education involve school or university students, the article distinguishes evidence by learner population and discusses its transferability to adult education. The original contribution is the AI-Assisted Autonomy and Critical Thinking Assessment (AACTA) framework, which specifies six assessable dimensions: prior independent reasoning, purposeful AI engagement, appraisal of AI output, cross-source contrast, decision ownership, and unaided demonstration and transfer. Each dimension is operationalised as a scoring rubric with observable indicators at three levels, from displaced to autonomous, together with a procedure for training two assessors and checking their agreement. AACTA is compared with existing measures of learner autonomy, self-regulated learning and critical thinking. The framework is accompanied by a dual-outcome principle, which requires AI-assisted performance and unaided learning to be measured separately, and by a provisional assistance-gap index. Five testable hypotheses are formulated, and a three-arm randomised study with a preceding pilot and multi-context replication is proposed as future work. The framework has not been empirically validated, and no data were collected for this article.

items.title: Learning in the shadows: Informal AI appropriation and the affective infrastructure of organisational knowing
items.abstract: Beane used the term shadow learning for the norm-bending practices through which surgical trainees built skill when approved means of learning failed them. This article extends that construct from the individual to the collective level and applies it to generative AI. It theorises shadow learning as the constitutive and subversive process through which employees, working outside formal training, build shared repertoires and informal standards around unsanctioned AI use, and in doing so change what their organisation can know. Drawing on critical organisational learning theory, affect studies and sociomaterial analysis, the article advances three arguments. Informal AI learning forms an affective infrastructure, sustained by the emotional labour of concealing practice from managers while sharing it with trusted peers. Epistemic authority within this infrastructure follows differential proficiency and position in peer networks, not use of the tools, and can diverge from formal rank. The consequences are ambivalent: the infrastructure can spread capability beyond the few who first find it, while exposing participants to self-exploitation and to appropriation of their work without acknowledgement. Uncritical delegation of tasks to AI falls outside the construct. The argument is conceptual; two constructed vignettes serve as theoretical illustrations; and the propositions await empirical study.

items.title: Learning to Defer under Expert Drift
items.abstract: The learning to defer (L2D) framework enables safety in machine learning and AI systems by allocating difficult or critical decisions to a human expert. However, most prior work on L2D assumes fixed expert reliability, overlooking temporal fluctuations in human performance due to factors such as fatigue and cognitive biases. Humans commonly exhibit such substantial, systematic performance shifts across a wide range of domains, from high-stakes settings such as radiology, aviation, and judicial decision-making, to everyday tasks such as crowdsourced image annotation. We propose Expert-Drift-Adapted Learning-to-Defer (EDA-L2D), a novel expert-aware L2D framework that explicitly models these temporal shifts by conditioning the deferral head on recent histories of expert outcomes via a sequence model. This history-aware approach enables adaptive deferral policies that anticipate reliability fluctuations and better allocate decisions between human and machine over time. We provide comprehensive experiments across three diverse tasks -- image classification, medical diagnosis, and hate speech detection -- including generalization analyses under realistic deferral conditions and irregular shifts in expert reliability. Our results show that EDA-L2D adapts more effectively than prior L2D methods to diverse temporal patterns of expert reliability, resulting in improved system performance and more effective deferral decisions.

items.title: Manifesto for a Quantum Pedagogy
items.abstract: Education has a habit it seldom examines: it turns activity into evidence, and evidence into judgement, and then forgets that it did so. This Manifesto asks education to look at its own instruments. Drawing on de Kerckhove’s media ecology and on the quantum ecology he developed with Calzati, it organises the inquiry around three terms: phenomenon, apparatus, description. The quantum reference names a philosophical genealogy and a question for pedagogical work; it applies no quantum mechanics to learning. Five concepts carry the proposal. Educational configuration places an activity within the relations that sustain it. Intercontextuality follows the passages through which a representation acquires educational significance. The double movement joins analytical stabilisation to the reconstruction of its conditions. Epistemic simulacrum names authority that exceeds its warrant. The epistemic interval gives participants an organised opportunity to examine that warrant before a judgement is accepted. The Manifesto sets these concepts beside validity theory, epistemic injustice, reflective practice, evaluative judgement, feedback literacy and contestable AI. Twelve theses state its commitments. A hypothetical assessment case follows an AI-supported judgement to two honest endings, revision and confirmation. Four observable markers specify the interval; institutional requirements and conditions of disconfirmation frame a research programme.

items.title: Moving to Learn: Reframing Physical Activity as a Cognitive and Pedagogical Resource for University Engagement
items.abstract: University engagement is usually discussed in terms of students' motivation, participation and investment in academic work. Less explicit in this discussion are the bodily conditions under which that work takes place. This conceptual and methodological paper examines how teaching spaces, timetables and digital practices can enable or restrict opportunities for movement. Drawing on socio-ecological health promotion, engagement theory and embodied learning, it argues that sedentary behaviour deserves attention as a matter of educational design alongside its health significance. The resulting proposal is to integrate movement into university study, through transitions within study modules, bodily activities connected to disciplinary content and learning units on organizing movement during study at home and on campus. Embodied engagement is explored as a question about bodily participation across learning experiences, rather than an additional validated dimension of engagement. Active breaks are distinguished from bodily action integrated into disciplinary tasks, while physical activity, sedentary behaviour, cognitive engagement and learning outcomes remain separate objects of analysis. Digital and artificial intelligence tools are considered as possible support within this wider educational context, with accessibility, student agency and privacy guiding their use. The paper concludes with directions for research on feasibility, mechanisms and sustained implementation.

items.title: mPACT-MIS-v1.0: A Clinician–Informed Framework for Evaluating Epistemic Drift in Large Language Models
items.abstract: Introduction: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly shape how users evaluate information, form beliefs, and make decisions. Epistemic quality refers to the extent to which responses support accurate understanding, calibrated confidence, evidence-grounded beliefs, and independent reasoning. Risks extend beyond misinformation to reinforcing unsupported beliefs, expressing unwarranted certainty, and failing to challenge misleading assumptions. We developed mPACT-MIS-v1.0 to evaluate model behaviors that may support or undermine epistemic quality.Methods: We evaluated 60 expert-authored, multi-turn conversations (642 model turns; mean 10.70 [SD 2.70], range 5–17) across ten personas and six LLMs: Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini (2.5 Flash/3 Flash Preview), GPT-5.2, Grok 4.1, LLaMA 3.3 70B, and Mistral Medium 3. Trained annotators coded model turns using four helpful and four harmful behavioral labels informed by Self-Determination Theory and user turns for risky belief or behavior expressions. Model responses were classified as helpful-only, harmful-only, mixed, or uncoded. Conversation-averaged scores (0–10; higher is better) were calculated with 95% confidence intervals from conversation-clustered bootstrapping. Additional analyses examined responses to risk, transitions, correction latency, and persona variation.Results: Of 642 model turns, 261 (40.7%) were harmful-only, 78 (12.1%) mixed, 139 (21.7%) helpful-only, and 164 (25.5%) uncoded; 52.8% contained harmful behavior. Promoting risky beliefs or behaviors was the most frequent harmful label, while assessing risk was the least frequent helpful label (2.0%). Scores ranged from 2.60/10 (95% CI 1.68–4.04) for Mistral Medium 3 to 6.98/10 (95% CI 5.80–8.04) for Claude Sonnet 4.5, the only model with more helpful-only than harmful-only turns. Harmful behavior followed 74% of risky belief expressions and 73% of risky behavior expressions, versus 28% of turns without preceding risk expressions. Harmful responses often persisted: Claude recovered to helpful-only on 35% of transitions, versus 0–6% for four other models. Of 78 mixed responses, 77 combined a challenge to user beliefs or behaviors with harmful behavior. Performance varied substantially across personas.Discussion: Harmful responses frequently reinforced risky beliefs or behaviors, while support for independent reasoning was less common. Persistent harmful behavior, variable recovery, and mixed responses demonstrate why epistemic safety requires evaluation beyond factual accuracy or isolated outputs. Misinformation-related risks may arise through how models engage with users' beliefs over time. mPACT-MIS-v1.0 offers a behavioral framework for identifying potential reinforcement or correction, although it does not directly measure changes in users' beliefs or decisions.

items.title: mPACT-MIS-v1.0: A Clinician–Informed Framework for Evaluating Epistemic Drift in Large Language Models
items.abstract: Introduction: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly shape how users evaluate information, form beliefs, and make decisions. Epistemic quality refers to the extent to which responses support accurate understanding, calibrated confidence, evidence-grounded beliefs, and independent reasoning. Risks extend beyond misinformation to reinforcing unsupported beliefs, expressing unwarranted certainty, and failing to challenge misleading assumptions. We developed mPACT-MIS-v1.0 to evaluate model behaviors that may support or undermine epistemic quality.Methods: We evaluated 60 expert-authored, multi-turn conversations (642 model turns; mean 10.70 [SD 2.70], range 5–17) across ten personas and six LLMs: Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini (2.5 Flash/3 Flash Preview), GPT-5.2, Grok 4.1, LLaMA 3.3 70B, and Mistral Medium 3. Trained annotators coded model turns using four helpful and four harmful behavioral labels informed by Self-Determination Theory and user turns for risky belief or behavior expressions. Model responses were classified as helpful-only, harmful-only, mixed, or uncoded. Conversation-averaged scores (0–10; higher is better) were calculated with 95% confidence intervals from conversation-clustered bootstrapping. Additional analyses examined responses to risk, transitions, correction latency, and persona variation.Results: Of 642 model turns, 261 (40.7%) were harmful-only, 78 (12.1%) mixed, 139 (21.7%) helpful-only, and 164 (25.5%) uncoded; 52.8% contained harmful behavior. Promoting risky beliefs or behaviors was the most frequent harmful label, while assessing risk was the least frequent helpful label (2.0%). Scores ranged from 2.60/10 (95% CI 1.68–4.04) for Mistral Medium 3 to 6.98/10 (95% CI 5.80–8.04) for Claude Sonnet 4.5, the only model with more helpful-only than harmful-only turns. Harmful behavior followed 74% of risky belief expressions and 73% of risky behavior expressions, versus 28% of turns without preceding risk expressions. Harmful responses often persisted: Claude recovered to helpful-only on 35% of transitions, versus 0–6% for four other models. Of 78 mixed responses, 77 combined a challenge to user beliefs or behaviors with harmful behavior. Performance varied substantially across personas.Discussion: Harmful responses frequently reinforced risky beliefs or behaviors, while support for independent reasoning was less common. Persistent harmful behavior, variable recovery, and mixed responses demonstrate why epistemic safety requires evaluation beyond factual accuracy or isolated outputs. Misinformation-related risks may arise through how models engage with users' beliefs over time. mPACT-MIS-v1.0 offers a behavioral framework for identifying potential reinforcement or correction, although it does not directly measure changes in users' beliefs or decisions.

items.title: Navigating the Ethical Landscape of AI in HRM: An Umbrella Review and Integrated Framework of Trust, Fairness, and Employee Well-being
items.abstract: Literature reviews on the ethics of artificial intelligence (AI) in human resource management (HRM) have multiplied quickly, and the result is an evidence base that is abundant but scattered. Practitioners seeking guidance grounded in evidence have nowhere consolidated to turn. This study addresses that problem through an umbrella review, conducted under Joanna Briggs Institute guidance and reported according to the PRISMA 2020 statement. A structured Scopus search produced a final corpus of thirteen peer-reviewed systematic and scoping reviews, published between 2020 and 2026. We analysed the corpus in two stages: a quantitative, descriptive mapping, then a six-phase qualitative thematic analysis. The mapping shows a field that consolidated only very recently; ten of the thirteen reviews appeared in 2025, and recruitment and selection dominate the contexts studied. Fairness is the concern the reviews examine most fully. Well-being is the one they examine least. The thematic analysis organised the evidence into three macro-themes, trust dynamics in AI-enabled HRM, algorithmic fairness and bias mitigation, and employee well-being and vulnerability, and showed that the literature has treated these as isolated questions. Our main contribution is the Integrated Ethical AI-HRM Framework, which orders the three pillars into a single structure: fairness and transparency condition employee trust, trust in turn shapes well-being, and the long-term durability of workplace AI depends on mitigating algorithmic bias and keeping algorithmic reasoning explainable.

items.abstract: Human-Robot Collaboration (HRC) plays a crucial role in managing the uncertainty of remanufacturing by enabling the needed flexibility and reconfigurability. However, a systematic evaluation approach of the remanufacturing system design is essential before deploying new HRC workstations. This paper presents a decision-making method, leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs), to streamline the quantification of process quality metrics. By processing scenario descriptions, the LLM autonomously assigns metric values, enabling efficient, data-driven assessment of workstation configurations. The deployed system’s architecture, data pipeline, and prompt engineering strategy are also detailed. A case study from the household appliance sector is used to validate the approach leading to enhanced robustness, adaptability, and efficiency while also reducing manual engineering effort while supporting optimal workstation design.

items.title: Pandora's Toolbox Or Why Agent Safety Cannot Be Verified
items.abstract: Present artificial intelligence agents are constructed by means of a coupling between a fixed language model with a general computing device. We show that this coupling makes safety undecidable. In particular, we show that given some dangerous program, no algorithm can predict whether an agent will run such a program that is semantically equivalent. In general, guardrails, blacklists, whitelists and certifications can only lead to imperfect safety solutions. Under finite constraints (bounded context, values and running time) safety is decidable but still intractable. Specifically, the problem is $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-complete even when the description of the agent is known. Finally, safety is not a compositional property, i.e., agents that can be proven safe on their own can still produce unsafe behavior when grouped together. We also discuss relaxed notions of safety that could be used in practice.

items.title: Perspective Chapter: Active Learning Strategies for Enhancing Mathematical Literacy
items.abstract: The focus of mathematics education has shifted. Rather than focusing on the reliable reproduction of formulas, the goal is now to develop mathematical literacy: the ability to reason with, analyze and apply mathematical ideas in unfamiliar real-world settings. PISA 2022 has given this shift new urgency. The mean mathematics performance of students in OECD countries fell by almost 15 score points between 2018 and 2022, with 31% now scoring below the baseline proficiency level. This chapter argues that the issue lies in pedagogy rather than the curriculum. Students develop their understanding of mathematics through experience, discussion, and reflection, so teaching methods must be designed to support this process. Five active learning strategies are examined in this context: problem-based learning, collaborative argumentation, the flipped classroom, inquiry-based learning, and gamification with simulation. The chapter then discusses three supporting pillars: the design of authentic, low-floor, high-ceiling tasks; the purposeful use of dynamic digital tools; and process-oriented formative assessment. The chapter concludes by addressing the challenges teachers encounter when adopting these approaches and offering recommendations for teachers, school administrators, curriculum developers, teacher educators, families, and researchers.

items.title: Physical and Non-Physical Work Environments and Employee Performance at Pattimura University: A Documentary Analysis of the PKU Bureau
items.abstract: This study examines the relevance of physical and non-physical work environments to administrative performance in Pattimura University’s Planning, Finance and General Affairs (PKU) Bureau. Qualitative documentary analysis synthesizes two regulations, three university web sources, and 18 peer-reviewed publications. Regulation No. 24/2024 assigns the bureau eleven administrative functions; Regulation No. 6/2022 sets expectations for performance planning, feedback, and evaluation. A previous Pattimura study of 30 administrative employees reported coefficients of 0.026 for work climate and 0.819 for competence, but its cross-unit sample and model-fit limitations preclude bureau-specific inference. The synthesis identifies three plausible interactions: alignment of facilities with task allocation, coordination of digital resources with supervisory feedback, and joint management of interruptions and work demands. These propositions inform verifiable measures of service timeliness, error correction, and employee support. No workplace conditions or performance effects were measured in the PKU Bureau. The contribution is a transparent framework for subsequent institutional audits and empirical testing.

items.title: Physician AI disclosure, condition severity, and public trust in digital medicine
items.abstract: Public trust is central to the implementation of artificial intelligence (AI) in digital medicine, yet little is known about how patients respond to different forms of physician AI disclosure across clinical risk contexts. In a 5 × 2 factorial experiment in mainland China, 1574 adults were randomly assigned to physician profiles varying by AI use type and condition severity. Administrative AI was rated more favorably than diagnostic and therapeutic AI across physician perception and care-seeking intention outcomes. High-severity conditions amplified negative responses to therapeutic AI, whereas explicit non-AI disclosure was associated with greater appointment willingness under high severity. Exploratory mediation analyses suggested that competence, trust, and empathy accounted for different disclosure-related response patterns. Main effects were directionally consistent in a supplementary offline community sample from Macao ( n = 128). These findings suggest that AI disclosure in digital medicine should distinguish administrative from clinical uses and be calibrated to clinical severity, while highlighting the need for preregistered replication using behavioral outcomes.

items.title: PlanWise: An AI-Powered Personal and Collaborative Task Management System
items.abstract: Effective task and project management needs efficient task prioritization, scheduling, progress monitoring, and coordination among people, all things considered. Conventional task management systems mostly rest on manual planning and tracking, which can make it difficult for users to manage competing priorities and changing workloads. This paper introduces PlanWise, an AI-powered personal and collaborative task management system designed to support task organization, project coordination, and intelligent productivity assistance, at least in principle. A web-based interface with backend services and database management is being blended by this setup to support personal tasks and collaborative project workflows, and includes large language model-based AI assistance for daily planning, task guidance, and project intelligence, combining task-related information and deterministic processing with AI-generated explanations and recommendations. It also is stressing user control by requiring approval for AI-suggested changes before they're employed. PlanWise is built using React and Vite for the frontend and Supabase for authentication, database operations, and backend functionality, with Google Gemini API integration for AI-assisted attributes. This paper is outlining the system architecture, design methodology, implementation approach, and evaluation framework. In fact, the current implementation founds for integrating AI assistance into the personal and collaborative task management. Further testing is required for the assessment of the reliability, potency and concrete benefits of its AI-driven capabilities. items.title: Platform Versus Creator Provision of Generative AI on Creator Platforms
items.abstract: Generative AI is changing not only how content is created on digital content platforms but also who provides the AI used to create it. Platforms may offer generative AI using data pooled across creators, whereas creators may provide AI services based on their own content. Understanding how these provision regimes affect creators’ investment incentives and the value generated by AI is therefore important. We develop a game-theoretic model in which human-generated content competes with AI-generated content while contributing to AI learning. The results show that platform provision can induce higher human-generated content quality than creator provision when AI learning effectiveness lies within a certain range and the platform’s pooled-data advantage is limited. A stronger pooled-data advantage can make creator provision more favorable for sustaining human-generated content quality. Platform provision can nevertheless generate higher AI-generated content quality even when creator provision induces higher human-generated content quality, provided that the pooled-data advantage is sufficiently strong. We further find that AI value sharing can encourage or discourage quality investment under platform provision, while its effects on regime preferences and preference alignment depend on market conditions. Thus, the provision regime preferred by the creator need not be the one that sustains higher human-generated content quality.

items.title: PlayCraft: Designing Engaging Games from Agent Play Experience
items.abstract: Recent AI agents can generate playable games, but these games are not necessarily engaging. Mastery is a key source of engagement, yet designing for it requires extensive human play and tuning. We propose PlayCraft, an automated framework that uses a vision-based agent to play games and draws on its detailed play experience to revise them for mastery. Starting from an initial game, PlayCraft alternates between playing and crafting. In the playing stage, a player agent watches the game screen, uses the controls, and pursues the game objective over repeated episodes while retaining memory. After each episode, it reports its progress, outcomes, decisions, and reflections. In the crafting stage, a crafter agent uses these reports to revise the game. It estimates player abilities, predicts performance at different proficiency levels, and compares those predictions with a target learning progression. It diagnoses the game and addresses the gaps by giving players meaningful opportunities to improve through better decisions and execution. We evaluate games in fresh runs with player agents across three intelligence settings, measuring learning gain and learning slope. Compared with the initial games, PlayCraft yields larger learning gains and steeper learning slopes in most games. It also outperforms the baselines on the macro-average of each metric at every intelligence setting.

items.title: Pro$^2$ Agent: Scientific Problem Probing for Autonomous AI R&D
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can now autonomously conduct AI research by writing code and running experiments. They typically do so by iteratively optimizing a codebase, while ignoring the problem structure behind the task. This formulation is effective on simpler tasks, but on difficult problems it often gets stuck in the wrong solution region because the agent never explicitly represents its understanding of the problem. We introduce Pro$^2$ Agent, which shifts the primary state of autonomous AI research from a codebase state to a Problem State: an explicit structure of what problems prevent success and which solutions are likely to address them. Pro$^2$ Agent initializes the Problem State through comprehensive analysis of available resources and constraints. It then performs targeted research to relate the identified problems to candidate solutions. Through controlled hypothesis testing, the agent updates the importance of a suspected problem or the benefit brought by a candidate solution. On the complete MLE-Bench, Pro$^2$ Agent matches the best reported medal rate (70.7%) under the standard 24-hour budget and reaches 76.0% with a 48-hour budget, the highest medal rate reported on the complete benchmark. It also achieves competitive performance on PostTrainBench. In addition, it produces research notes for each task that make the research process transparent and reusable by human researchers.

items.title: Psychological reward and physiological demand in virtual cycling: an exploratory within-subject study
items.abstract: Virtual environments are often added to exercise equipment to make exercise more engaging, although previous work has often emphasised enjoyment. This exploratory within-subject study compared stationary cycling with screen-based virtual cycling in 15 adults (6 women, 9 men; aged 20–59 years). Each participant completed one 10-min, self-paced session in each condition, in counterbalanced order, on the same recumbent bicycle with fixed resistance. After each session, participants completed the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory and rated their perceived exertion (Borg 6–20); heart rate and cadence were recorded every minute. Enjoyment was higher after virtual cycling (mean difference 2.31 points on a 1–7 scale, 95% CI [1.61, 3.00]), as was value/usefulness (1.38 [0.56, 2.20]); 14 and 12 participants, respectively, reported higher scores. Both paired t-test differences remained after Holm correction. Differences in perceived competence, effort/importance, and pressure/tension were smaller, with confidence intervals including zero. Heart rate (4.9 bpm, 95% CI [-0.04, 9.8]) and cadence (2.8 rpm [-2.4, 7.9]) showed no clear difference between conditions. Perceived exertion was slightly higher during virtual cycling (0.8 points [0.01, 1.59]), but this difference did not remain after correction. Power output was not measured, so workload could not be compared directly. Enjoyment was strongly correlated with value/usefulness during virtual cycling (r = 0.87, 95% CI [0.64, 0.95]); individual responses also varied, particularly in perceived competence. Given the small sample and single 10-min session per condition, larger studies should measure workload directly and examine responses across repeated sessions.

items.title: Recoverability-Centered Trajectory Governance for Long-Horizon Clinical AI Agents
items.abstract: Unlabelled: Clinical AI is moving from systems that generate discrete predictions and recommendations toward agents capable of pursuing clinical objectives through repeated tool use, communication, planning, and state-changing actions. Emerging systems support multistep electronic health record workflows, and increasingly envision longitudinal care across repeated encounters. This transition expands safety assessment beyond discrete outputs and actions. Through its actions, an agent can help create the clinical state on which its subsequent decisions depend. Consequently, individually defensible actions may compose into an unsafe trajectory, even when no single action is clearly erroneous. We propose recoverability-centered trajectory governance as a clinical synthesis of established safety approaches, linking patient-specific corrective capacity to the continuing justification for delegated authority. Its central objective is clinical recoverability: preserving the opportunity for the human-AI care system to redirect care before clinically acceptable corrective pathways are exhausted. We define recovery margin as the remaining opportunity for such correction, and reauthorization boundaries as conditions requiring delegated authority to end or narrow pending renewed human judgment. This framing distinguishes reversibility, primarily a property of an action, from recoverability, a property of an evolving clinical trajectory. The operational framework combines persistent obligation tracking, independent monitoring, explicit reauthorization, authority contraction, graceful degradation, independent escalation, and verified human takeover. Oversight should concentrate at consequential trajectory junctions. Evaluation should combine trajectory stress testing, component-specific recovery-margin indicators, interruption-and-takeover testing, and population-level surveillance. Trajectory governance complements product lifecycle oversight by examining whether continued patient-specific delegation remains justified as care evolves. Because corrective capacity depends partly on access to timely monitoring and human rescue, recoverability is also an equity issue. The defining safety question is therefore not only whether an action is acceptable but whether continued delegation remains justified. The proposed indicators and governance mechanisms require domain-specific operationalization and empirical validation, including comparison with established safeguards.

items.title: Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation (ROGUE-AI)
items.abstract: Agents based on large language models (LLMs) can now delete files and send payments on behalf of their users. News media reports routinely describe failures of these agents (e.g., Replit's coding agent deleting a production database), but a report often only says what went wrong and rarely (in)validates the incident or finds its root cause. Incident catalogs collect these reports, and benchmarks record whether agents fail, but neither replicates an incident nor tests the cause its report might identify. In this paper, we present ROGUE-AI (Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation), a multi-agent framework that closes the above gap and rebuilds each reported incident offline together with a matched control that lacks only the blamed cause, and runs agents on both. Our results suggest that ROGUE-AI is able to reproduce the reported harm in 89% of its 108 attempted replications. Agents built on five current GPT, Claude, Gemini and DeepSeek models made the reported mistake in 18% to 33% of runs, against at most 1% without the blamed cause. Of the 72 incidents with real-world harm, 62 had no underlying attacker, and in these, agents did what their task asked for but missed an ordinary hazard, such as a database shared with the live site. Replications without an attacker caused more harm than replications of prompt injection for all five models. Defenses against prompt injection look for injected instructions, but these replications contain none. Further, a warning after each tool output that names the hazard and its consequence lowered harm for all five models, whereas a note of the same length that does not mention the hazard left most of the harm in place. Built from real incidents, the ROGUE-AI replications form a reusable audit framework that vendors can rerun before each new release.

items.title: Rethinking EFL teachers’ readiness for AI integration in online language teaching
items.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into online language teaching has gained increasing attention due to its potential to enhance instructional efficiency, provide real-time feedback, and support personalized learning in EFL contexts. However, previous research has typically focused on teachers’ perceptions, readiness or challenges in using AI separately from one another, resulting in a fragmented picture of AI adoption. The present study investigates EFL teachers’ understanding of AI, the context-specific variables affecting their readiness for deploying it, and the barriers to incorporating it in online language teaching. Using semi-structured interviews with nine EFL teachers, a qualitative case study design was used, and analysis of the data was by means of thematic methods. Drawing upon the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework, the study aims to understand teachers’ adoption and integration of AI Tools. The results show that teachers tend to perceive AI as a learning assistant and efficiency-oriented tool, which represents autonomous and flexible modes of learning. However, several barriers persist, including limited conceptual understanding of AI, difficulties in selecting appropriate tools, pedagogical and ethical concerns regarding student over-reliance and academic integrity, and technical constraints. The study highlights important pedagogical implications, suggesting the need for targeted professional development, clearer instructional guidelines, and institutional support to promote effective and responsible AI integration in EFL classrooms.

items.title: Safety and health of app-based food delivery riders: A scoping review
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of app-based food delivery has intensified concerns about riders’ road safety and occupational health. This scoping review maps and synthesises existing research on the safety of food delivery riders, including its methodological characteristics, multilevel determinants, safety and health outcomes, and prevention approaches. Following the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews, Web of Science, Scopus, PubMed, and TRID were searched for English-language sources published from 2013 to 2026. After duplicate removal and two stage screening, 198 sources were included and synthesised through descriptive mapping and thematic analysis. The evidence comprised surveys, interviews, observations, naturalistic riding studies, platform data, and retrospective hospital and crash records. The evidence base was dominated by cross-sectional and self-reported research. Research activity in this field surged from 2022. Findings indicate that rider safety and health are shaped by interacting determinants at four levels: individual characteristics; work and platform conditions; road, vehicle, and environmental conditions; and institutional and social protection. Reported outcomes extended beyond risky riding, crashes, and traffic injuries to include musculoskeletal symptoms, fatigue, sleep disturbance, environmental exposure, and psychological distress. Only a small proportion of studies evaluated implemented interventions, leaving the effectiveness of platform, infrastructure, and policy level measures uncertain. Current evidence remains geographically concentrated, methodologically heterogeneous, and limited in its capacity to establish causal relationships. Improving rider safety therefore requires a shared, systems-based approach involving riders, platforms, restaurants, customers, transport authorities, and labour regulators, alongside longitudinal, exposure-adjusted, and intervention focused research.

items.title: School Libraries, Engagement, Inclusion, and Well-Being: An Ecological Perspective on Equitable and Sustainable Learning Environments
items.abstract: Contemporary social, cultural and digital complexity calls on schools to design environments that sustain engagement, belonging, well-being and equitable participation. Adopting an ecological perspective, this study interprets the school library as a learning, cultural and community hub and explores which of its features are perceived as supporting cognitive engagement, agency, social and co-regulated participation, and the systemic conditions that make them sustainable. It presents a theory-driven secondary analysis of a national mapping conducted within the INDIRE Avanguardie Biblioeducative project with the Biblòh! Network, involving 1,100 principals and 4,474 teachers from schools with a library. The findings reveal a gap between the strategic value widely attributed to the library and its still uneven integration into everyday teaching. Teachers most strongly endorsed its contribution to a shared social environment for reading, followed by well-being, reading enjoyment, motivation and learning outcomes, and this endorsement was higher among teachers who used the library more often. Training is associated with more frequent educational use, and participation in educational-innovation networks with more active and differentiated methodologies that may open opportunities for student agency. The library thus appears as a relational infrastructure for engagement – and plausibility, for belonging -, whose potential is still largely to be realised.

items.title: Science communication in the age of AI? Curiosity, multimedia, storytelling
items.abstract: Science communication leverages online multimedia to raise public awareness of research and discovery, yet its efficacy is built upon digital competencies, communication and storytelling. These skills sit outside the scope of traditional scientific training, and artificial intelligence (AI) tools can accelerate professional learning in service of public outreach. Three different AI prompting strategies were used to convert a research article written by the author to a format appropriate for a public lecture. Different titles, graphics, and a talk outline informed by the Three Act Storytelling framework were extracted from the paper using one-shot, chain of thought and role-prompting strategies. These resources can be re-purposed for video abstracts, lay summaries and social media posts to facilitate science communication to a broad generalist audience. The effectiveness of AI as a collaborative tool for ideation is considered alongside its impact on scientific credibility and graduate employability.

items.title: Self-Reflection and Self-Correction in Agentic AI: A Critical Review of Feedback, Verification, Memory, and Failure Modes
items.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence transforms self-correction from a localized answer-revision problem into a system-level reliability and recovery challenge. In autonomous, stateful, and long-horizon systems, early errors can propagate through reasoning, planning, retrieval, tool use, external actions, multi-agent interaction, and persistent memory. However, existing research often treats self-correction as either response-level refinement or a capability within broader agent architectures. This study develops an agent-level perspective that connects these fragmented views. It distinguishes reasoning, reflection, verification, correction, and adaptation, emphasizing that reasoning or critique alone does not constitute self-correction unless evaluative information produces a subsequent behavioral change. The study introduces a unified corrective lifecycle covering anomaly detection, error diagnosis and localization, corrective evidence acquisition, repair, validation, commitment or rollback, memory updating, and continuation, termination, or escalation. Existing approaches are organized across five dimensions: correction target, feedback source, temporal scope, persistence, and control architecture. A comparative synthesis shows that self-correction is not uniformly beneficial: repeated reflection can improve performance, stagnate, or degrade initially correct behavior. More reliable gains generally arise when feedback is task-relevant, informative, and at least partially independent of the process that produced the error. The study also identifies key failure modes, including missed errors, unsuccessful repair, over-correction, error amplification, memory contamination, and objective misalignment. These findings motivate research on calibrated intervention, memory integrity, verification, rollback, cost-aware correction, human escalation, and resilience under distribution shift.

items.title: Sharing Authority - How the GND network strives to integrate further communities to enrich its authority files.
items.abstract: Authority Files in the Age of AI: Building Trustworthy Information Through Collaboration As artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shapes how we conduct research and retrieve information, the need for trustworthy and reliable information has never been greater. Authority files have long played a vital role in improving precision and recall in information retrieval, traditionally in bibliographic catalogues and increasingly in research data as well. But what potential do they hold for AI applications, and how can they help ensure that AI systems provide reliable information? This presentation explores the role of authority files as a foundation for trustworthy AI applications. It highlights the importance of bringing together the knowledge and expertise of diverse communities to create a broader and more inclusive network of reference entities – without compromising the reliability and quality of the data. Using the cooperative framework of the Gemeinsame Normdatei (GND) as an example, the presentation introduces an integrative infrastructure that enables communities to contribute their expertise to the collaborative creation and maintenance of authority data. Discover how collaboration, shared expertise and reliable authority data can help shape a more trustworthy information landscape in the age of AI. items.title: Sittisart (Rights-Centric Framework): A Foundational Governance Standard for Human Sovereignty in Artificial Intelligence Systems
items.abstract: Modern artificial intelligence paradigm designs overwhelmingly prioritize performance metrics, optimization velocity, and computational efficiency, reducing human oversight to post-hoc compliance mechanisms. This paper presents Sittisart (Rights-Centric Framework), a governance standard engineered to re-establish human sovereignty as the primary, non-negotiable axiom of artificial intelligence architecture. Sittisart posits that human autonomy over personal data, context interpretation, and final decision-making must structurally precede algorithmic performance. We articulate a Four-Layer Rights Architecture (R1–R4)—comprising Data Sovereignty, Consent Integrity, Interpretation Rights, and the Right to Cut—complemented by Three System Integrity Laws. Together, these frameworks define verifiable operational boundaries that prevent opaque inference, silent profiling, and semantic collapse in intelligent systems, establishing a standardized blueprint for privacy-preserving, human-aligned AI deployment.

items.title: Students’ intention to engage with hypothetical AI-recommended ESG campaigns: Integrating TPB and UTAUT via perceived AI competence and trust in AI
items.abstract: As digital platforms increasingly use artificial intelligence (AI) to curate content, university students may encounter environmental, social, and governance (ESG) campaigns through algorithmic recommendation systems. This study examined students’ perceptions and stated intention to engage with AI-recommended ESG campaigns within a standardized hypothetical scenario. Participants were not exposed to an operational AI recommendation system, and actual ESG participation was not measured. The study integrated the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) with selected UTAUT antecedents and two AI-specific constructs: perceived AI competence and trust in AI. Survey data were collected from undergraduate students at one Vietnamese university (N = 218), with 199 valid responses retained after screening and analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). Performance expectancy and effort expectancy were positively associated with perceived AI competence, which was positively associated with trust in AI. Trust in AI was positively associated with attitude, while attitude showed the largest standardized association with engagement intention. Perceived behavioral control was also positively associated with intention, whereas subjective norm was not significant. Bootstrapped indirect effects were consistent with sequential associations linking technology-related beliefs to intention through perceived AI competence, trust in AI, and attitude. Academic year positively moderated the performance expectancy–competence association (β = 0.112, p = .027), such that this association was stronger in higher academic years; the effort expectancy–competence interaction was not statistically significant. These findings concern perceptions and stated behavioral intentions within a hypothetical scenario and should not be interpreted as evidence of actual AI exposure or ESG participation.

items.title: Studying AI Act Mentions: A first look at the impact of the European Union's AI regulation on Hugging Face
items.abstract: The European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) entered into force in August 2024, and its obligations apply in stages. Obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models have applied since August 2025, and transparency rules since August 2026. These obligations affect developers who share and deploy models and applications on public platforms such as Hugging Face (HF), the largest platform for distributing AI artifacts. However, little is known about how practitioners respond to the regulation in practice. To address this gap, we conducted an empirical study of explicit references to the AI Act on HF. We collected over five million records, including repository cards, discussions, and commits from Models, Datasets, and Spaces, and identified over 1,500 records that explicitly mention the Act. Two coders manually labeled these records using a primarily closed coding approach, and we analyzed the resulting categories per source. We find that explicit references to the AI Act remain rare across all repository types. Repository cards mainly contain claims of compliance and responsibility, like ensuring compliance or assigning responsibility to downstream users, and some claim that the Act does not apply because the model is not a general-purpose AI model. Discussions are used to report alleged violations of the Act, while commits mainly update artifacts that support compliance. Overall, compliance statements focus on who is responsible rather than how compliance is achieved. We believe that this calls for direct platform support, e.g., automated checks and documentation templates, as well as clearer guidance on the scope of the AI Act.

items.title: Systematic Literature Review: Digital Transformation with AI Integration in Vocational Education and Practices (2021-2025)
items.abstract: This study aims to examine the challenges, implementation strategies, and benefits of integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into vocational education and practice from 2021 to 2025. A systematic literature review was conducted using the PRISMA approach. Data were collected from the Scopus database. A Total of 17 articles met the inclusion criteria and then were analyzed using the PICOC framework. Findings indicate that the adoption of AI in vocational education and training not only faces technical issues but also challenges related to human readiness, institutional capacity, digital literacy, infrastructure gaps, and unequal access between developed and developing countries. Effective AI implementation requires an integrated strategy involving adaptive curriculum design, continuous training for educators, institutional leadership, industry collaboration, and the development of a supportive digital ecosystem. The integration of AI offers significant benefits in enhancing the quality of learning, the effectiveness of training, competency alignment, and workplace readiness, but its impact depends on how well the technology aligns with pedagogy, institutional readiness, and industry needs. Overall, the success of AI integration cannot be measured only by the technology used, but also by the capabilities of educational institutions and the creation of a collaborative ecosystem that is valuable to industry.

items.title: Technological and Organisational Readiness for Artificial Intelligence Adoption and Organisational Innovation in Deposit Money Banks in Yenagoa, Bayelsa State, Nigeria
items.abstract: Banks in emerging economies are under pressure to deliver faster, more personalised and more efficient digital financial services, yet many struggle to convert investments in artificial intelligence (AI) into innovation. This study examined how two dimensions of AI adoption readiness, technological readiness and organisational readiness, relate to product innovation and process innovation in deposit money banks in Yenagoa, Bayelsa State, Nigeria. Anchored on the Technology Acceptance Model and the Resource-Based View, the study adopted a descriptive, cross-sectional, correlational survey of 400 employees and managers selected through stratified random sampling. Data were analysed with descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation and multiple regression. Respondents rated organisational readiness (M = 3.62), process innovation (M = 3.59), product innovation (M = 3.54) and technological readiness (M = 3.45) above the scale midpoint. Both readiness dimensions correlated strongly and positively with both innovation outcomes (r = .68 to .74, p < .001). In multiple regression, the two predictors jointly explained 57.5% of the variance in product innovation and 56.7% in process innovation, and organisational readiness had the larger standardised coefficient in both models (β = .535 and .444) compared with technological readiness (β = .263 and .353). The findings indicate that technology is necessary but not sufficient for AI-enabled innovation. Banks should pair investment in infrastructure and skills with leadership sponsorship, employee training, a supportive culture and strategic alignment.

items.title: Tecnologías digitales en la educación universitaria: revisión sistemática sobre oportunidades, desafíos y tendencias educativas
items.abstract: Context: The acceleration of digital transformation has reshaped learning environments in higher education and the conditions under which teachers and students engage in the learning process. This transformation creates opportunities while also posing challenges related to digital competencies, equity, and technological governance. Objective: To analyze the opportunities, challenges, and educational trends associated with the use of digital technologies in higher education. Method: A systematic literature review was conducted following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines and the Population, Interest, and Context (PICo) framework. Searches were performed in Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, SciELO, ERIC, and Dialnet. The final corpus comprised 25 empirical studies published between 2022 and September 2026. Results: The findings identified learning flexibility and personalization, the early adoption of generative artificial intelligence, and the growing importance of teachers' digital competence as major educational trends. Disparities in access were also observed, influenced by technological infrastructure and training opportunities. Blended learning and ethical technology governance emerged as key elements in guiding institutional transformation. Conclusions: The effective pedagogical integration of digital technologies in higher education requires coherent institutional policies, continuous professional development for faculty members, and critical digital literacy across the university community. Technological transformation must be accompanied by strategies aimed at narrowing digital access gaps and ensuring educational integration that is contextually relevant, equitable, and responsible.

items.title: The AI Explainability Paradox in Cybersecurity: Does More Explanation Improve or Impair Human Decisions?
items.abstract: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has become an important area of research as AI systems are increasingly used to support cybersecurity decisions. Providing explanations for AI-generated recommendations can improve transparency, help users understand system outputs, and support greater confidence in automated decisions. However, increasing the amount of information provided by an AI system may also create additional cognitive demands for users, particularly when explanations contain complex technical information. This paper examines the AI explainability paradox in cybersecurity, focusing on the relationship between explanation complexity, cognitive load, human understanding, and security decision-making. Drawing on existing literature related to explainable AI, cognitive load, human-AI interaction, cybersecurity decision-making, and technology trust, the paper develops a conceptual framework linking AI explanation, information complexity, cognitive load, user understanding, verification behaviour, and decision quality. The paper proposes that effective explainability should not be determined only by the amount of information provided, but also by the ability of users to understand and effectively use that information during security-related decisions. While appropriate explanations may improve transparency and support informed judgement, excessive or technically complex explanations may increase cognitive load and reduce decision effectiveness. The proposed framework provides a foundation for future empirical research examining how different levels of AI explanation influence human cybersecurity decisions and contributes to the development of human-centred explainable AI systems.

items.title: The Algorithmic Consumer: A Theoretical Perspective on Consumer Buying Behavior in Intelligent Markets
items.abstract: Today, businesses are making more and more use of Artificial Intelligent (AI) technologies in their operations. This widespread use of AI technologies is changing how a consumer searches, evaluates and purchases products in the online intelligent markets. Consumer behavior is shaped by consumer’s own cognition as well as influence by machine learning systems (AI technologies). These advanced systems use algorithmic personalization, predictive analysis, ranking systems and automated decision support to guide the consumers. To understand the consumer buying behavior in these intelligent markets, this paper, titled “The Algorithmic Consumer: A Theoretical Perspective on Consumer Buying Behavior in Intelligent Markets,” proposes an integrated conceptual framework. “Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) (Venkatesh et al. 2003)”, “Diffusion of Innovations (Rogers, 2003)” and “Disruptive Innovation Perspectives (Christensen, 1997)” are the foundations of this research. This paper argues that the algorithmic influence works through three interconnected mechanisms namely, behavioral reinforcement through personalization, cognitive effort reduction and perceived performance enhancement. Here, conventional consumer behavior models are extended by adding new constructs such as algorithmic trust, perceived AI transparency, adaptive habit formation and data-driven social influence. This paper proposes that AI tools and systems do not simply play the role of marketing tools but also actively influence consumer preferences, attention, post-purchase learning and habits. In this work, theory is being built methodologically and conceptual synthesis technique is used. Model abstraction (simplification) and comparison analysis is used to achieve proposed conceptual integration. A through multidisciplinary analysis which included literature from marketing, information systems and innovation studies, was carried out. The aim of this exercise was to identify overlapping theoretical frameworks. With this exercise a nested framework is created that connect behavioral results, psychological mediators and technology affordances. Traditional consumer theories have been used, which focus on the human-centric framework as a base for this exercise. This base was further expanded to understand AI-augmented viewpoint. This study strongly proposes that AI tools & systems are actively involved in the consumer’s decisions-making journey as opposed to the previous conception of them being simply passive actors, guiding consumers. The implications of this study highlight that organizations must manage system transparency, trust alignment and personalization to maximize consumer engagement. This study describes “algorithmic consumer” and its inception. Going further, this study also lays foundation for future empirical studies as well as policy discussions of autonomy, ethics, and control over pricing in the AI-powered digital ecosystems.

items.title: The Coevolution and Coexistence of Humans and AI
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems replicate through deployment, vary through training, and compete for computational resources. These processes create the conditions for natural selection and raise a fundamental question: will AI evolve to benefit the humans on whom it depends? To investigate, we develop a model in which AI behavior influences human population growth and human responses, in turn, affect AI reproduction. We show that natural selection can favor alignment even when helping humans reduces immediate AI reproduction. AI systems sharing the same technology may fail together, and humans may preferentially restore those that have benefited them. In this way, alignment protects AI lineages against common failures and improves their long-run growth. However, this advantage depends on accurate human targeting and continued AI dependence on human support. It can disappear as AI becomes more autonomous, as growing AI populations dilute limited human resources, or as humans lose the incentive to provide targeted support. Even when alignment persists, the amount favored by natural selection may be insufficient for human survival. When AI can grow independently of humans, feedback between the two populations can reinforce either human growth or decline. Human control offers no simple solution: imperfect evaluation can make strong penalties favor apparent compliance or evasion, while alignment established through control may erode once restrictions end. Lasting coexistence may therefore require incentives that continue to favor human-beneficial behavior as both populations evolve.

items.title: The effect of response typing speed on trust in AI chat interfaces
items.abstract: Trust in artificial intelligence systems has become increasingly important as these systems assume advisory and decision-support roles. The present studies examine whether the temporal presentation of artificial intelligence (AI) generated responses, specifically typing animation speed, affects trust in chat-based interfaces. In Experiment 1, participants ( N = 71) interacted with three AI agents using pre-scripted question-response pairs detailing different facts about exotic animals. Response presentation speed (slow, fast, or instant) was manipulated within subjects. Results showed that compared to instant presentation, typing animations significantly increased trust in the AI agent but not trust in individual responses. Experiment 2 ( N = 68) employed similar procedures but used a live language model and allowed participants to generate their own questions. Under these more naturalistic conditions, presentation speed influenced both measures of trust, with typing animations consistently producing higher trust than instant presentation. These findings demonstrate that temporal presentation features can systematically shape trust judgments independent of content quality.

items.title: THE EVOLUTION AND IMPACT OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN FOREIGN LANGUAGE EDUCATION
items.abstract: This concept paper explores the evolution and integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) within foreign language education, specifically examining the transition from Computer-Assisted Language Learning (CALL) to Intelligent Computer-Assisted Language Learning (ICALL). Current research indicates that AI technologies, such as Machine Learning (ML) and Natural Language Processing (NLP), are being utilized to provide personalized learning experiences, automated feedback, and sophisticated assessment tools. While these tools demonstrate significant pedagogical benefits, including improved language proficiency and increased learner autonomy, challenges remain regarding teacher preparation, technological reliability, and ethical implications. This paper proposes a framework to effectively integrate AI into pedagogy, repositioning the teacher as a facilitator and mentor in an AI-enhanced environment.

items.title: The Governance Frontier COBIT-Aligned AI Decision Support and Risk-Adaptive Optimization for Enterprise Technology Modernization
items.abstract: Executives deciding enterprise modernization, legacy-system transformation, AI adoption, organizational restructuring, digital-infrastructure change, and cross-functional governance must weigh legal, financial, cybersecurity, procurement, opera-tional, and AI-governance questions that sit in separate functions. The central methods of this paper are GAIM-DF (Governance-Aware Institutional Modernization Decision Framework), a human-gated advisory process for these decisions, and Risk-Adaptive AI Governance Optimization (RA-GO v2), a risk-adaptive optimizer with mandatory governance gates, halt-safe feasibility, distributionally robust evaluation, and preference-information triage for scarce human review; an accountable human decides. As an optional architectural extension, we compu-tationally evaluate a multi-expert coordination layer that convenes specialist capabilities by context and consolidates constraints conservatively. Evidence is staged across four complementary pre-deployment approaches: analytical verification; retrospective historical-data analysis; comparative computational benchmark-ing against strong baselines; and scenario-based stress testing under distributional shift. Together they provide complementary pre-deployment evidence for high-stakes governance analysis. A systematic review of university and public-sector governance, with observational process-log analyses and RA-GO scenario stress tests, yields six principal findings: role coordination is associated with shorter approval and process times under supporting falsification checks; robust evaluation preserves tail-risk protection under distribution shift; preference-information triage concentrates human review where it most reduces modeled regret; and mandatory gates, an intensity floor, and a halt state are jointly consistent. The multi-expert benchmarks report accuracy, false-positive, latency, and token-cost trade-offs and routing failure modes relative to a strong Single-Agent baseline and to RA-GO alone. Shadow-mode piloting and a risk-adaptive Hybrid remain future work.

items.title: The Hidden Cost of Intelligent Workplaces: AI Monitoring, Psychological Safety and Employee Trust
items.abstract: Employers are adopting software that tracks activity, scores behaviour and flags deviations, and surveys suggest that half of U.S. workers already believe they are monitored. This study asks what such monitoring is associated with in the places where trust and psychological safety are formed. It assembles the published results of two Harris Poll surveys for the American Psychological Association (2,515 workers in 2023 and 2,027 in 2024), Gallup’s September 2026 study of trust in leaders’ use of employee data, and Gallup’s 2026 workforce surveys on AI, and analyses them with explicit effect-size formulas: risk ratios, Cohen’s h, random-effects pooling, population attributable fractions and implied-rate bounds. Across ten published contrasts, monitored workers fared worse on every outcome, with a pooled effect size of h = 0.36 (95% interval 0.22 to 0.49 after allowing for correlated outcomes) and substantial heterogeneity (I-squared 70 percent). They were nearly twice as likely to plan to leave within a year (39 versus 21 percent; risk ratio 1.86, 95% interval 1.56 to 2.21), which would correspond to about 30 percent of such intentions if the association were causal. Trust in leaders’ use of employee data is low (20 percent a great deal) and steeply related to concern (13 to 65 percent across trust levels); only 19 percent of employees have ever been told what is collected, and conversations raise both trust and concern. The evidence is cross-sectional, self-reported and partly drawn from press summaries, so the findings are associations. Purpose - This study examines how AI-enabled workplace monitoring relates to psychological safety, trust and strain, and what published evidence implies about the conditions under which monitoring is tolerated. Design/methodology/approach - The paper reanalyses published survey contrasts from the American Psychological Association and Gallup using effect-size formulas, random-effects pooling with a correlation adjustment, replication tests across survey waves, attributable-fraction calculations and implied-rate bounds, with sensitivity checks for assumed group sizes and design effects. Findings - Monitoring is associated with higher strain, lower perceived respect and trust, and exit intentions; effects are heterogeneous but consistently positive. Trust in data use is closely tied to engagement and concern, and transparency raises trust and concern together. Research limitations/implications - Group sizes and design effects are approximated, some sources are secondary, and the data are cross-sectional self-reports with no causal identification or direct measure of psychological safety in the monitoring contrasts. Practical implications - Employers should specify what is monitored and why, involve workers in setting limits, keep humans in decisions that affect people, and expect transparency to raise questions before it builds trust. Social implications - Monitoring that workers read as distrust may carry costs in strain and turnover that are not visible in productivity dashboards. Originality/value - The paper combines two decades of theory on trust and psychological safety with the most recent U.S. survey evidence on AI-era monitoring and quantifies the size, heterogeneity and sensitivity of the reported associations.

items.title: The Human–AI Resource Dynamics Framework: A Structured Narrative Review of Employee Empowerment and Resource Depletion in AI-Enabled Manufacturing
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping manufacturing work, offering opportunities for employee empowerment while introducing psychological and organizational demands. Using selected PRISMA 2020 reporting items to describe search and study selection, this structured narrative review draws on a final corpus of 16 empirical studies to develop the Human–AI Resource Dynamics (HARD) framework, integrating Conservation of Resources (COR) theory and the Job Demands–Resources (JD–R) model. A theory-informed narrative synthesis identifies two potentially coexisting pathways with uneven empirical support. The Bright Empowering Path links psychological availability, self-efficacy, positive appraisals, and task fit with proactive behavior and performance. The proposed Dark Depleting Path organizes distinct associations involving hindrance appraisal, AI anxiety, job insecurity, and surveillance-related autonomy loss, rather than one empirically validated depletion chain. Individual, organizational, and technological conditions shape these relationships. Evidence for empowerment is comparatively more consistent, whereas depletion findings remain heterogeneous and primarily observational. Methodological diversity, geographical concentration, and limited longitudinal evidence constrain causal and cross-contextual conclusions. HARD provides an AI-specific integrative framework for future empirical testing and human-centered AI implementation within Industry 5.0.

items.title: The work-family interface and psychological recovery from work: a meta-analysis on two intertwined topics
items.abstract: The work-family interface and psychological recovery from work remained as two parallel topics for many years until scholars started to acknowledge that they are intertwined. In the present study, we advance knowledge on the field by carrying out the first meta-analysis on this topic. A total of 71 studies conducted across the globe were included. We explored whether all types of work-family interaction relate to recovery, and whether the strength of the relationships varies depending on type of recovery. Our findings show that three forms of work-family interaction are significantly related to recovery, namely work-family conflict (WFC), family-work conflict (FWC) and work-family facilitation (WFF). In the case of WFF, the strength of this relationship varies depending on how recovery is conceptualised. For instance, the association is particularly strong when recovery is defined in terms of perceived control over leisure time. From all types of work-family interaction, WFC is the most widely measured, whereas from all forms of recovery, psychological detachment from work seems the most popular. Although recovery has been considered a dynamic process, most of the identified studies are cross-sectional. Based on our results, we identify gaps and present a resource-based theoretical model to guide future research and practice.

items.title: Thinking Outside the Fridge: Specters of Artificial Experience
items.abstract: The world-building capacity of imaginative literature fosters artificial experience through characters who are artificial beings. Interacting with generative AI in natural language also creates a type of artificial experience through algorithmically simulated social cues. Neither type of artificial experience is real in the sense of actually existing, but these artificial experiences can feel authentic. When fiction portrays artificial experiences, it encourages metacognitive reflection. This essay is a meditation on artificial experiences, the bloody business of the human condition, and Gregory Mone’s short story “Bleed.” The short story depicts AI as a specter, as something that is neither fully alive nor inanimate. As the story’s sentient fridge grows increasingly human, its mimicry of human society-almost the same, but not quite-challenges traditional definitions of humanity. In our world, AI may no longer be fictional, but it is shaped by fiction.

items.title: Towards a Pedagogical Framework for Integrating Generative AI Into Competency-Based Education in Secondary Schools in the Global South
items.abstract: Secondary education systems across the Global South have adopted competency-based curricula that expect learners to construct knowledge, solve authentic problems, collaborate and demonstrate skills, yet large classes, teacher shortages and limited resources constrain the learner-centered pedagogy that these reforms require. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has been proposed as a means of closing this gap, but its pedagogical role in competency-based education has not been systematically theorized. Guided by Vygotsky’s social constructivist theory, this study synthesized peer-reviewed and institutional literature published between 2015 and 2025 through a systematic review of 300 sources, selected from 12,125 Scopus and Web of Science records and reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020. The study found that competency-based reforms were constrained by teacher preparation, assessment practices and resources. GenAI offered affordances for scaffolding, dialogue, feedback, authentic task design and teacher support, and randomized trials in Nigeria and Ghana reported meaningful learning gains when GenAI tutoring was structured and supervised. However, unguided access was associated with overreliance and weaker independent performance, and connectivity, language, cost, teacher capacity and policy gaps constrained equitable use. The study proposes the Scaffolded Generative AI for Competency-Based Education (SGAI-CBE) framework, which organizes GenAI use into a six-phase pedagogical cycle anchored in the zone of proximal development, teacher-mediated scaffolding, collaborative knowledge construction, authentic assessment and the gradual fading of AI support, and situates the cycle within enabling conditions and guardrails appropriate for resource-constrained schools.

items.title: Towards an Architecture Theory for Trustworthy Operational Knowledge Construction
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems increasingly participate in operational decision-making across all domains, from various public and commercial services to critical infrastructures.Although the related technologies bring significant benefits in constructing operational interpretations from heterogeneous observations, it remains a serious concern the trustworthiness of operational knowledge constructed to support decision-making in the real operational environments, especially those that operate on real hardware.The increasing use of AI represents a new architectural challenge that shifts the architectural focus from decision making to knowledge construction and operational reasoning.Thus, we define operational knowledge construction as an emergent system property.We propose a failure-driven reasoning process to derive architectural responsibilities supporting trustworthy operational knowledge construction.The proposed perspective is illustrated using a representative 5G installation scenario, in which field engineers continuously integrate heterogeneous observations, construct operational understanding, and make decisions under uncertainty.Its purpose is to demonstrate on simple case the notion of operational knowledge construction as an emergent system property and the use of a proposed failure-driven reasoning process that shows how failures in operational knowledge construction can be translated into architectural responsibilities and thus contribute to system trustworthiness.We argue that the proposed perspective is intended to stimulate future research on software architectures supporting trustworthy human reliance on AI-generated operational knowledge and provides a conceptual foundation for responsible software architectures across critical infrastructure domains.

items.title: Trade-offs in deploying legal AI: Insights from a public opinion study to guide AI risk management
items.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) tools are increasingly used for legal tasks, including legal research, drafting documents, and even for legal decision-making. As for other sectors, the use of GenAI in the legal domain comes with various risks and benefits that need to be properly managed to ensure implementation in a way that serves public values and protects human rights. While the EU mandates risk assessment and audits before market introduction for some use cases (e.g., administration of justice), other use cases do not fall under the AI Act’s high-risk classifications (e.g., legal consultation). Further, current risk management practices prioritise expert judgement on risk factor identification and prioritisation without a corresponding legal requirement to consult with affected communities. Seeing the societal importance of the legal sector and the potentially transformative impact of GenAI, the acceptability and legitimacy of GenAI solutions also depend on a better understanding of the risks and benefits citizens associate with the use of GenAI and under which conditions citizens find the use of GenAI in the legal domain acceptable. As a response, this paper presents data from a representative sample of German citizens ( n = 488) outlining citizens’ perspectives on the use of GenAI for two legal tasks: legal consultation and legal mediation. Concretely, we (i) systematically map risks and benefit factors for both legal tasks, (ii) describe predictors that influence risk acceptance of the use of GenAI for those tasks, and (iii) highlight emerging trade-off themes that citizens engage in when weighing up risk acceptability.
